notes.meaning: David warns us not to get worked up or jealous when bad people seem to do well. To "fret" means to get heated and burn inside. Feelings like that can tempt us to copy the wicked. Their success is short, like grass that soon dries up in the sun.

Instead of envying, trust God and do good, and keep the two together. Matthew Henry says it is not trusting God but testing Him if we trust and then live as we please. "Dwell in the land" means living quietly in the place God gives. Older Bibles add the promise "thou shalt be fed," and some read it as feeding on God's faithfulness.

To delight in the Lord is to find our deepest joy in Him. The promise is not that He will grant every passing wish. It is about the desires of a heart God has made new: to know, love and please Him. A person who truly enjoys God comes to want what God wants, so these desires are safe to grant.

"Commit" literally means "roll." Picture rolling a heavy load onto someone much stronger. We bring all our cares to God in prayer, do our duty, and leave the outcome with Him. He will act on our behalf.

Good people are sometimes misjudged or falsely blamed. God promises to make their honesty plain, like dawn breaking through the night and growing to full noon. This may happen in this life, and at the latest on the final day of judgment. If we keep a clear conscience, we can trust God with our good name.

"Be still" literally means "be silent" before the Lord. It is not a sulky silence but a trusting one that stops complaining. Waiting here is not doing nothing. It is eager, hopeful looking to God. So do not stew over schemers whose plans seem to work.

Let go of anger, whether it is aimed at the wicked or at God. Fretting only leads to harm. Bitterness can tempt us to do wrong ourselves, perhaps by copying the wicked to get ahead, or by acting rashly.

Two reasons are given for not fretting. The success of evildoers will soon end, and those who hope in God will inherit the land. "The land" first meant Canaan, the land God promised Israel. It stands for all of God's covenant blessings, that is, the good things He has bound Himself by promise to give His people. Wesley notes this was mostly fulfilled literally in Israel's day.
Be patient, because it will not be long. The wicked person who seems so important will be gone. You may look for his house, his position and his wealth, and find nothing left.

The "meek" are people who bear hardship and wrongs patiently, without envy or anger. Jesus repeats this promise in Matthew 5:5. They may not have great wealth. But they will enjoy something better: deep peace, peace with God and peace within.

The wicked plot against good people and grind their teeth in rage. But God laughs at their plans. This is not because He does not care. He already sees the day of judgment coming for them, and their malice cannot finally win.

The wicked do more than plot. They take up weapons, and sword and bow stand for every kind of violence. They aim at the poor and needy, meaning God's people, and at honest folk who never did them harm. That shows how cowardly and cruel they are.

Evil turns back on itself. The weapons the wicked made for others end up wounding them. Spurgeon points to Haman, who was hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, and to Saul, who fell on his own sword.

A little with God's blessing is better than great heaps of wealth without it. The good person's little comes from God's loving hand, is used well, and brings peace. The Hebrew word for the riches of the wicked hints at noise and turmoil. That stands in contrast with the quiet of a humble, godly home.

The "arms" of the wicked stand for their power to do harm, and that power will be broken. Someone with broken arms can neither hurt others nor help himself. God Himself holds up the righteous, the people who live right with Him.

God knows every day of His people's lives, the bright ones and the dark ones. He watches over them with loving care and knows what dangers they face. What they will receive from Him does not fade but lasts forever, as a lasting home with God in heaven.
Hard times will come, but God's people will not be put to shame for trusting Him. Even in famine He will provide what they need. Or He will give them content hearts, as He fed Elijah in the drought.

The wicked will vanish like the beauty of the fields and like smoke that thins out and is gone. Older Bibles say "as the fat of lambs." That fat was burned up completely on the altar and rose as smoke. Their glory has no real substance.

The wicked borrow and do not pay back. Some refuse, and some have grown so poor they cannot. The righteous are generous and give freely. God has shown them mercy, and He gives them the means to help others.
What makes the difference is God's blessing or His curse. Those He blesses will enjoy the land and all its good. Those under His curse will be cut off.

The Lord makes the steps of a good person firm and guides them. He often leads step by step, the way a child is led. He takes pleasure in that person's path, like a parent watching a child's first steps.
A good person may stumble and fall, but will not stay down for good. God holds their hand, giving them something firm to grip so they can get up again.

differ.view: A true believer may fall into sin for a time. But God's grace brings him back to repentance, and he can never be finally lost.
The "fall" here means falling into trouble, not into sin. Believers stay safe as they keep trusting and obeying God.

notes.meaning: Looking back on a long life, David says he never saw God abandon the righteous or their children reduced to a life of begging. Readers have taken this as a general rule from long experience, not a promise with no exceptions. Matthew Henry notes that Jesus taught us to expect hardship when we suffer for His sake.
Good people are kind all day long and ready to lend to those in real need. Their children are blessed and become a blessing. God often repays generosity in the next generation.

Turn away from evil and do good. Both matter, and we turn from evil first. The promise is a settled, lasting home. It does not mean we earn eternal life by good works. God's grace, His undeserved kindness, gives the strength to do both.
The Lord loves justice and never abandons His saints, His faithful people, in their troubles. He keeps them safe forever. But children who follow their wicked parents' ways will be cut off like them.

The same promise comes up again: the righteous will inherit the land and live there forever. The repetition gives it weight. Since no one stays on this earth forever, Matthew Henry sees it fulfilled at last in heaven, the better land that Canaan pictured.
A good person's words are wise and fair. What we say shows what is in our hearts. Such a person talks about God's ways and stands up for what is right.

God's law is not just outside rules for this person. It lives in their heart because they love the God who gave it. Wise words and steady steps flow from that. Adam Clarke links it to God's promise to write His law on His people's hearts.

The wicked watch for a chance to destroy good people. But God will not leave them in their enemy's power. Even if people condemn them, God, the highest Judge, will clear them. Matthew Henry also applies this to Satan, the accuser, who cannot win against God's people.

Wait for the Lord and keep walking in His way: wait and walk together. Our part is to obey, and the outcome is God's. In time He will lift His people up to enjoy what He promised, and they will see the wicked removed.

David tells what he himself saw. A cruel, powerful man was spreading out like a great tree in its native soil, seemingly rooted for good. Then suddenly he was gone, and no trace of him could be found.

Now watch the blameless and upright, the sincere and wholehearted, and see how their lives turn out. Older Bibles read "the end of that man is peace": whatever storms come, it ends well. The word can also mean "future" or "descendants." Adam Clarke and Keil & Delitzsch take it that way, which is why the BSB says "posterity awaits."

differ.view: God can make a believer "perfect" in heart in this life, saving him from all sin and filling him with His love.
No one is perfect in themselves. Believers are counted perfect because they are joined to Christ.

notes.meaning: All who rebel against God will be destroyed together, with none left out. The wicked have no future worth having. Their hopes and their line end.

Salvation, God's rescue in every danger and finally into His glory, comes from the Lord, not from the righteous themselves. Spurgeon calls this the heart of the good news of free grace. In trouble God is their safe refuge and strength.

The Lord helps His people bear their troubles and in time rescues them from the wicked. He does this not because they have earned it. It is because they have placed their trust in Him. The psalm that began with fretting ends in quiet trust.
